processing: Orthodox Darjeeling processing for the black teas, with lighter oxidation in spring as is usual. Manufacture has taken place at Turzum since the two gardens merged.
harvest_season: As usual in Darjeeling, first flush in spring and second flush in early summer, then monsoon and autumn; the garden sells a range of named clonal lots too.
appearance_dry: Typical of Darjeeling, wiry olive-and-brown leaf with pale tips, greener in clonal spring lots.
appearance_liquor: Pale gold in spring and clonal lots, amber in summer.
appearance_wet: Tender green-and-copper leaf in spring, browner in later flushes.
taste_profile: As is typical for the district, floral and brisk in spring and fruitier in summer; clonal lots usually lean more aromatic.

brewing.notes: Western-style. Use about 85°C for first flush and clonal lots.

vintage_note: Sold by year and flush, and also under clonal names such as Himalayan Mystique and Clonal Delight. Spring and clonal lots are best within about a year of picking. Check the flush and whether the tea is black, green, oolong or white, as the garden makes all four.
description:
Sungma is a Rungbong Valley garden at 1,100 to 1,700 metres, in the Jorebunglow Sukhiapokhri block, with 281.95 hectares under tea. It is run together with neighbouring Turzum, and both names appear on lots.

The range is wider than most: black, green, oolong and white tea, plus tea flower and named clonal lots like Himalayan Mystique, Clonal Enigma and Clonal Wonder. It also appears on lists of organic Darjeeling gardens.

For the black teas, expect the district's usual arc of flowers in spring and fruit in summer. Keep the water cooler for spring and clonal lots.

When you buy, check the exact tea type and flush, as the name alone covers very different cups. Part of the Jay Shree group, it sits alongside Puttabong and Balasun, which makes for easy comparison.
history:
British planters established Sungma between 1863 and 1868, and Turzum (Tarzum) dates from the same decade. The 1934 earthquake destroyed the Sungma factory, after which the two gardens were merged and all manufacturing moved to Turzum.

The garden now belongs to Jay Shree Tea & Manufacturing, of the B.K. Birla Group.
